author: KERNAL Content Team
title: Deploying ML Models
subtitle: Saving models, building APIs, and serving predictions

whyItExists.problem: A trained model sitting on a data scientist's laptop provides zero business value. It needs to be accessible to applications and users in real time — accepting new inputs and returning predictions within milliseconds.
whyItExists.solution: Model deployment packages a trained model and its preprocessing pipeline as a REST API endpoint that any application can call over HTTP.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When you're ready to put a model into production. Even if you're just prototyping, a local FastAPI server lets you test the model end-to-end before full deployment.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For batch predictions over large datasets, a REST API is wasteful — load the model directly in a script and run predictions on the entire dataset at once.

explainModes.beginner: Once a model is trained, you save it to a file (like saving a document). Then you wrap it in a small web server that listens for requests. When an app sends features over the internet, the server loads the model, runs the prediction, and sends back the result.
explainModes.simple: Model deployment: save the trained model with joblib, write a FastAPI server that loads the model on startup, define an endpoint that accepts feature values in a JSON request body, runs the model, and returns the prediction.
explainModes.standard: Production deployment requires: serialising the model and all preprocessing objects (scaler, encoder) with joblib, an API server (FastAPI) that validates inputs, applies transformations, and returns predictions with proper error handling, plus Docker for reproducible containerisation.
explainModes.technical: The deployment artefact must include the full inference pipeline: imputer → encoder → scaler → model. Use Pydantic for input validation. Version the API (/v1/predict). Containerise with Docker for environment reproducibility. CI/CD deploys on passing tests.
explainModes.deepDive: Production ML serving has two modes: online (low-latency single-row predictions via REST API) and batch (high-throughput bulk scoring via batch jobs). Canary deployments roll out new models to a fraction of traffic first. Shadow mode compares new model predictions against the live model without affecting users.

content.text: Deployment is the step that turns a trained model into business value. The workflow: save the model and preprocessing pipeline → build an API that loads them → containerise with Docker → deploy to a server or cloud service.
Always save the complete preprocessing pipeline alongside the model. If you trained on scaled features but deploy only the model (without the scaler), predictions will be completely wrong.

content.code:
import joblib
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
import os

# Build a Pipeline that includes preprocessing
pipe = Pipeline([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler()),
    ('model', GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=200))
])
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Save to a versioned directory
os.makedirs('models/v1', exist_ok=True)
joblib.dump(pipe, 'models/v1/pipeline.joblib')
joblib.dump(X.columns.tolist(), 'models/v1/feature_names.joblib')  # save column order

print(f'Model saved. Test score: {pipe.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}')

# Load later
loaded_pipe = joblib.load('models/v1/pipeline.joblib')
feature_names = joblib.load('models/v1/feature_names.joblib')

payload = {
    'age': 42.0,
    'income': 75000.0,
    'tenure_months': 24,
    'num_products': 2,
    'has_credit_card': 1
}

response = requests.post('http://localhost:8000/v1/predict', json=payload)
result = response.json()

print(f'Prediction:  {result["prediction"]}')    # 0 or 1
print(f'Probability: {result["probability"]:.3f}') # P(class=1)
print(f'Status:      {response.status_code}')      # 200 = OK

content.text: Always save the scaler, imputer, and encoder objects alongside the model — not just the model weights. Predictions on unscaled or un-encoded data will be completely wrong.

Model drift: when real-world data distributions change over time, your model's performance degrades silently. Set up monitoring to compare prediction distributions and actual outcomes. Retrain when performance drops below your threshold.
FastAPI automatically generates interactive API documentation at /docs (Swagger UI). This lets you test endpoints directly in the browser without writing any extra code.

questions.question: Why must you save the scaler alongside the model?
options: Because production inputs must receive the same transformation that was applied during training
questions.explanation: The model learned from scaled features. If you feed unscaled production data to the model, it will produce wildly wrong predictions. The same scaler (with the same fitted mean/std) must transform all inputs.

questions.question: What is model drift?
options: When a model takes too long to make predictions
When model performance degrades over time because real-world data distributions change
When a model is transferred to a different server
When model weights change during deployment
questions.explanation: Model drift occurs when the statistical properties of the input data change over time (data drift) or when the relationship between inputs and the target changes (concept drift), causing the trained model to become less accurate.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of using a sklearn Pipeline for deployment?
options: It makes the model train faster
The entire preprocessing + model is saved as a single object — no risk of mismatching scaler and model versions
It adds validation logic to the API
questions.explanation: A Pipeline bundles all preprocessing steps and the model together. Saving the whole pipeline as one joblib file ensures the scaler, encoder, and model are always in sync — you can't accidentally use the wrong version.

faq.a: Model performance degrades over time because the real-world data distribution changes. For example, a fraud detection model trained on 2024 patterns may miss new fraud techniques in 2025. Monitor predictions vs actual outcomes and retrain regularly.

faq.q: Should I use Flask or FastAPI for ML APIs?
faq.a: FastAPI is the modern choice: it's significantly faster, generates automatic OpenAPI docs at /docs, validates inputs with Pydantic, and supports async out of the box. Flask is simpler but slower and lacks automatic validation.

faq.q: What is the difference between online and batch serving?
faq.a: Online serving (REST API) returns predictions in real time for individual or small groups of inputs — used for interactive applications. Batch serving runs predictions over large datasets on a schedule — used for overnight scoring or bulk processing.
